# Retrieval Strategies for Medical Question Answering

## Abstract

This paper compares three conditions for answering medical questions with a large language model: a vanilla LLM, a retrieve-then-read model, and RAG without reranking. The study uses MedAnswerSet as its main benchmark and measures hallucination frequency for each condition. Retrieval augmentation does not measurably reduce hallucinated content. The abstract gives a brief overview of the design and the quantity measured, so that readers can decide whether the full study is relevant to their work.

## Introduction

Large language models are now used to answer questions in clinical and biomedical settings. Their answers are often fluent, but they can contain statements that are not supported by any source, and such statements are a concern wherever the answers inform decisions about health. Researchers and practitioners therefore need clear evidence about how different answer procedures behave when the questions are medical in nature.

Several procedures differ in the material that the model receives before it answers. Some procedures give the model only the question, while others add documents that were looked up for each question. The available comparisons often vary several factors at once, so the role of any single procedural choice is hard to isolate.

The aim of this paper is to compare conditions that differ in how supporting documents are supplied to the model. The three conditions are a vanilla LLM, a retrieve-then-read model, and RAG without reranking. Each condition is evaluated on the same questions, so that differences in the measurements can be traced to the procedure rather than to the question set. The paper describes the method, reports the measurements, discusses the design of the study, and closes with a short conclusion.

## Method

Three conditions were defined for this study. In the vanilla LLM condition, the model is prompted with the question and nothing else. In the retrieve-then-read model condition, the system looks up supporting documents for each question and reads them before it answers. In the RAG without reranking condition, the system uses the same retriever but keeps the passages in their original order.

All three conditions were run on MedAnswerSet, which is the main benchmark of this study and contains 1,000 questions. The same questions were used in every condition, and the generator was held constant across conditions, so that the procedure is the only intended difference between them. Prompts were written once and reused for all questions.

The outcome is hallucination frequency, expressed in percent. It is defined as the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts. Each answer was assessed against the reference material for its question using a fixed rubric. A single rater applied the rubric to every answer, and the rater did not see the condition label during scoring.

## Results

MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark, was used for all three conditions. The table below reports hallucination frequency (%) for each condition on that dataset. Each entry is the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts.

| System | hallucination frequency (%) |
|---|---|
| vanilla LLM | 29.9 |
| retrieve-then-read model | 21.4 |
| RAG without reranking | 47.2 |

## Discussion

The design of this study has several limitations. First, only one benchmark was used, so the conclusions apply directly only to questions of the kind contained in MedAnswerSet. Second, the outcome depends on a judgement about whether an answer contains invented facts, and a single rater may apply that judgement differently from another rater. Third, all conditions share one generator, so the findings may not carry over to models trained on different data.

The retriever was also fixed in advance. The study compares one retriever under different handling of its passages, and it does not evaluate alternative retrievers or alternative ways of building the document collection. These choices keep the comparison focused, but they narrow the scope of the study.

The reference material for each question was taken from a single collection, and the questions were not stratified by topic. Both features bound the populations to which the study can be applied.

## Conclusion

This paper compared three conditions for answering medical questions on MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark. Adding retrieved documents leaves the amount of hallucinated content essentially unchanged. The findings rest on one dataset and one rater, and they should be read with those limits in mind.

# Comparing Four Answering Conditions on a Biomedical Claim Benchmark

## Abstract

This study compares four answering conditions on a biomedical question-answering benchmark and reports the hallucination rate of each condition on the same questions. Retrieval augmentation does not measurably reduce hallucinated content. The underlying model and the question set are held fixed across conditions. BioClaimQA is used as the main benchmark.

## Introduction

Language models answer biomedical questions fluently, yet a fluent answer can include statements that the published literature does not support. Several strategies have been proposed for this problem, including supplying the model with external passages, asking it to write out its reasoning, and rewriting questions before they are searched. These strategies differ in what the model sees and in how it produces an answer, and they are often evaluated on different collections, which makes their reported numbers hard to compare.

The aim of this study is to compare four conditions on a common benchmark, so that the hallucination rate of each condition can be read against the others. BioClaimQA is the main benchmark in this study. Its questions were written to require specific biomedical claims, and each answer can be checked against a short list of reference passages.

## Method

Four conditions were compared. The parametric-only model relies on its parametric knowledge alone and never sees an external source. The retrieval-augmented generator is given the top passages of a dense retriever together with the question. The chain-of-thought prompting condition is asked to write out its reasoning before giving the final answer. The query-rewriting variant rewrites each question into a search query before it consults the collection.

All four conditions use the same underlying language model, the same decoding settings and the same 1,000 questions from BioClaimQA. Keeping these elements fixed means that the procedure described above is the only difference between conditions. Decoding was run once per question, and no condition received additional tuning on the evaluation questions.

The hallucination rate is the percentage of answers that contain at least one unsupported statement. A statement counts as unsupported when none of the reference passages for that question entails it. Two annotators judged each answer, and a third annotator resolved any disagreement. The annotators saw the question and the answer text, but not the condition that produced the answer. Reference passages were fixed before any answer was generated, so that no condition could draw on passages chosen after its answers were known.

## Results

The table below gives the hallucination rate of each condition on BioClaimQA, with one row per condition.

| System | hallucination rate (%) |
| --- | --- |
| parametric-only model | 30.1 |
| retrieval-augmented generator | 22.4 |
| chain-of-thought prompting | 39.4 |
| query-rewriting variant | 38.3 |

## Discussion

The study uses one main benchmark, so its scope is limited to the question style and reference passages of BioClaimQA. The same four conditions could be applied to other biomedical collections to test whether the protocol transfers. Annotation relied on a small team, and deciding whether a statement is unsupported remains a human judgement that cannot be fully audited.

All conditions share one underlying model, which keeps the comparison controlled but limits how far the results can be generalised to other models. Decoding was run once per question, so variation across repeated runs was not measured. A later study could repeat decoding several times and report the spread of each hallucination rate.

## Conclusion

This study compared four answering conditions on BioClaimQA, using one fixed model and one set of questions. Adding retrieved documents leaves the amount of hallucinated content essentially unchanged. Further work should extend the comparison to additional benchmarks and to more than one underlying model, and it should report the variability across repeated decoding runs.

# Prompting and Source Access in History Question Answering

## Abstract

This paper compares four conditions for answering history questions with a language model: a closed-book model, a RAG pipeline, RAG with random passages, and chain-of-thought prompting. The study uses HistoryQuest as its main benchmark and measures the unsupported-answer rate for each condition. Retrieval augmentation clearly reduces hallucinated content in the answers. On HistoryQuest, the RAG pipeline reaches 27.4% unsupported-answer rate.

## Introduction

History questions are a common test of whether a language model can recall facts accurately, and the answers are often long enough to contain several claims that each need a source. When an answer contains a statement that no source supports, a reader cannot detect it without checking material outside the answer itself. Unsupported statements are therefore difficult to find in practice.

Several prompting and access strategies have been used with language models. Some rely only on what the model learned during pre-training, some provide documents from a reference collection, and others ask the model to write out its reasoning. Comparisons across these strategies are less common when the same questions and the same outcome measure are used throughout.

The aim of this paper is to compare conditions that differ in how the model is prompted and in what material it can access. The four conditions are a closed-book model, a RAG pipeline, RAG with random passages, and chain-of-thought prompting. Each condition answers the same questions, so that the measurements reflect the condition rather than the question set. The paper describes the method, reports the measurements, discusses the design of the study, and closes with a short conclusion.

## Method

Four conditions were defined for this study. The closed-book model answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. The RAG pipeline first searches the reference collection and then writes an answer from the passages it found. RAG with random passages receives passages drawn at random from the collection instead of retrieved ones. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving the final answer.

All four conditions were run on HistoryQuest, the main benchmark, which contains 1,000 questions. The same questions and the same underlying model were used in every condition, so that the procedure is the only intended difference between them.

The outcome is the unsupported-answer rate, expressed in percent. It is defined as the proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source. Each answer was checked by a single annotator against the reference collection and marked as unsupported when at least one statement could not be traced to a source.

## Results

HistoryQuest, the main benchmark, was used for all four conditions. The table below reports the unsupported-answer rate (%) for each condition.

| System | unsupported-answer rate (%) |
|---|---|
| closed-book model | 33.5 |
| RAG pipeline | 40.2 |
| RAG with random passages | 36.4 |
| chain-of-thought prompting | 13.1 |

## Discussion

The design of this study has several limitations. The study uses one benchmark, so its conclusions apply directly only to history questions of the kind contained in HistoryQuest. Each answer was judged by a single annotator, and a second annotator could draw the boundary of an unsupported statement differently. Each condition was run with one underlying model, and results may differ for models trained on other data.

The reference collection was also fixed for all conditions. The study therefore does not examine how the size, coverage or quality of the collection shapes the measurements, and it does not explore alternative search methods. These choices keep the comparison focused, but they narrow its scope.

## Conclusion

This paper compared four conditions for answering history questions on HistoryQuest, the main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to fewer hallucinated answers. The findings come from one benchmark, one annotator and one model, and they should be read with those limits in mind.

# Comparing Conditions for Unsupported Statements in History Question Answering

## Abstract

Language models often produce statements that no source supports, which limits their use in research and education. This paper compares several conditions for answering history questions on the HistoryQuest benchmark, using the unsupported-answer rate as the outcome measure. The conditions differ in whether the model can access documents, which passages it receives, and how it is prompted. Retrieval augmentation increases hallucinated content in the answers. The paper describes the design of the comparison and reports the unsupported-answer rate for each condition.

## Introduction

Large language models answer questions from knowledge learned during pre-training, and they can state facts that are unsupported or wrong. Several strategies have been studied for this problem, such as adding a reference collection as a source and prompting the model in different ways. Because these strategies are often evaluated on different benchmarks and with different measures, their results are difficult to compare directly. The aim of this paper is to compare conditions side by side on a shared benchmark and a shared measure, so that differences between conditions can be read from the same measurements. The comparison keeps the language model, the questions and the scoring procedure the same across conditions.

## Method

HistoryQuest is the main benchmark of this study. It contains 1,000 questions about historical events, people and dates, and each question is paired with a reference answer set that is used for scoring. All conditions answer the same questions in the same order.

The following conditions are compared. The closed-book model answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents, and is denoted by its code B. The RAG pipeline first searches the reference collection and then writes an answer from the passages it found, and is denoted by its code R. The RAG with random passages condition receives passages drawn at random from the collection instead of retrieved ones, and is denoted by its code A1. The chain-of-thought prompting condition asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving the final answer, and is denoted by its code A2.

The outcome measure is the unsupported-answer rate, abbreviated UAR. It is the proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source, expressed in percent. Each answer is split into individual statements, and an answer is counted toward the unsupported-answer rate when any of its statements is not backed by any source in the reference collection.

All conditions use the same language model, decoding settings and answer format, so that the conditions differ only in the input they receive. Answers are generated with greedy decoding, and every condition receives the same instruction asking for a short answer in plain prose. Prompts were fixed before the runs began and were not revised after any results were seen.

Scoring uses a fixed claim-checking procedure. The answer is broken into atomic statements, and each statement is checked against the reference collection by a separate verifier. The verifier was chosen before the study and was not tuned on HistoryQuest. Annotators checked a sample of verifier decisions, and disagreements were settled by discussion before the scores were computed.

Each condition was run on every question, and the unsupported-answer rates were computed over the full set of answers. No question was removed after the runs were complete, and the order in which the conditions were run was fixed in advance.

## Results

HistoryQuest is the main benchmark, and the table below reports the unsupported-answer rate for each condition on it. Each row names one system by its code, and the value column gives its UAR in percent.

| System | UAR (%) |
| --- | --- |
| B | 33.5 |
| R | 40.2 |
| A1 | 36.4 |
| A2 | 13.1 |

## Discussion

This study has several limitations that bear on how its comparison should be read. It uses a main benchmark, HistoryQuest, and its questions cover only a limited range of historical topics. The reference collection is held fixed for all conditions, so the comparison does not cover other collections. Scoring depends on an automated verifier that was only spot-checked by annotators, so some errors in claim checking are likely to remain. The language model, decoding settings and prompts were held constant, and the study does not examine other models or other prompt designs.

## Conclusion

This paper compared conditions for answering history questions on HistoryQuest, using a shared outcome measure and a shared scoring procedure for all of them. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to more hallucinated answers. Future work should test the same conditions on additional benchmarks and with other language models, so that the comparison can be repeated beyond this study.

# Comparing Answer Generation Conditions on History Questions

## Abstract

This paper compares four answer generation conditions on a shared set of history questions. HistoryQuest serves as the main benchmark, and every condition is scored with the same unsupported-answer rate and the same judging rubric. Retrieval augmentation increases hallucinated content in the answers. The design keeps the question set, the prompts and the annotation procedure fixed across conditions, which allows the conditions to be read side by side.

## Introduction

Question answering systems built on large language models are often judged by whether their answers are supported by evidence. Some deployed systems pair a generator with a search over a document collection, while others answer only from what the model learned during pre-training. Comparisons between these designs are hard to read when the question sets, the prompts and the scoring rules differ from one report to the next.

The aim of this study is to compare conditions that differ in how they access documents, together with a prompting condition that asks for written reasoning. Each condition is run on the same questions and scored with the same rubric. The study reports its results on HistoryQuest, which is the main benchmark of the paper, and it treats the rubric as an object of careful description rather than as an established standard.

## Method

The study compares four conditions. The closed-book model answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. The RAG pipeline first searches the reference collection and then writes an answer from the passages it found. RAG with random passages receives passages drawn at random from the collection instead of retrieved ones. Among the four conditions, chain-of-thought prompting is asked to write out its reasoning before giving the final answer.

All conditions answered the same 1,000 questions drawn from HistoryQuest. The unsupported-answer rate is defined as the proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source. Two annotators read each answer against the collection and marked every statement they could not trace to a source. Where the annotators disagreed, a third reader reviewed the answer and the majority mark was kept.

The prompts were identical across conditions, except for the instruction that each condition requires. Sampling settings were held fixed, and each answer was produced once. The rubric was written before any answers were collected and was not revised during annotation.

## Results

Each value below is reported for one condition on HistoryQuest, using the unsupported-answer rate.

On HistoryQuest, the closed-book model has an unsupported-answer rate of 33.5%. On HistoryQuest, the RAG pipeline has an unsupported-answer rate of 40.2%. On HistoryQuest, RAG with random passages has an unsupported-answer rate of 36.4%. On HistoryQuest, chain-of-thought prompting has an unsupported-answer rate of 13.1%.

## Discussion

The study uses one main benchmark, so its observations describe history questions in particular. Annotation depends on whether a reader can trace a statement to a source, which leaves room for disagreement even with a third reader involved. Each condition was run once per question, and no repeated runs were made to estimate variation between runs. The prompts were written by the authors and were not tested with other wordings. A fuller design would add more datasets, a larger pool of annotators and repeated runs for every condition.

## Conclusion

This paper compared four answer generation conditions on HistoryQuest, the main benchmark, under one shared rubric. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to more hallucinated answers. Further work should extend the comparison to other question sets and to additional annotation protocols.

# Lookup Steps and Invented Facts in Medical Question Answering

## Abstract

This paper compares three conditions on MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark of the study. The outcome is the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts, and every condition is judged with one procedure. Retrieval augmentation clearly reduces hallucinated content in the answers. The question set, the judging guide and the decoding settings were held fixed across conditions.

## Introduction

Medical question answering systems are expected to avoid invented facts, yet published reports often use different question sets and different judging rules, which makes them hard to compare. This paper sets out a controlled comparison of three conditions that differ in whether and how they look up documents before answering. The aim is to compare these conditions on one shared set of questions and one judging procedure.

The study is framed around a single main benchmark. The purpose of the design is to make the conditions comparable with each other, not to rank particular systems against published baselines.

## Method

The plain generator with no lookup step is prompted with the question and nothing else. The configuration that looks up supporting documents finds supporting documents for each question and reads them before it answers. The retrieval variant that skips the reranker uses the same retriever but keeps the passages in their original order.

Each condition answered 1,000 questions from MedAnswerSet. A judge marked an answer as containing invented facts when one of its statements could not be checked against the sources supplied with the question. The fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts was then computed for each condition. Judges worked from a single written guide, and a random sample of answers was judged twice to check agreement.

The judging guide and the prompts were fixed before any answers were collected. The same decoding settings were used for every condition, and no condition received tuning that the others did not receive.

## Results

Each value is reported below in one sentence.

On MedAnswerSet, the plain generator with no lookup step has a fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts of 299 out of 1,000. On MedAnswerSet, the configuration that looks up supporting documents has a fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts of 21.4%. On MedAnswerSet, the retrieval variant that skips the reranker has a fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts of 0.472.

## Discussion

The study relies on a single main benchmark, and judging depends on people deciding whether a fact is supported by the sources given. Judges worked under time limits, and only a sample of answers was checked twice, so agreement is known only for that sample. The conditions also differ in more than one detail at once, so the design cannot separate the contribution of each detail. Only one retriever was used, and the reranker variant was not tried with other retrievers. Further studies would need more judges and more datasets before the comparison could be widened.

## Conclusion

This paper compared three conditions on MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark, under one judging procedure. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to fewer hallucinated answers. Future work should test the same conditions on other medical question sets with a larger panel of judges.

Medical and open-domain questions place different demands on a language model. Medical answers must avoid invented facts, while open-domain answers are often compared with a reference text by overlap of words. Both kinds of answer also take time to produce, and the cost of an answer is not always reported alongside its quality.

Several strategies have been proposed. Some answer from the prompt alone, while others look up supporting documents before they answer, and the order of those documents may also differ between systems.

The aim of this paper is to compare conditions that differ in whether the model looks up documents before it answers and in how those documents are ordered. Each condition is evaluated on both datasets, so that the measures can be read side by side.

## Method

The vanilla LLM is prompted with the question and nothing else. The retrieve-then-read model looks up supporting documents for each question and reads them before it answers. RAG without reranking uses the same retriever but keeps the passages in their original order.

MedAnswerSet, the main benchmark, contains 1,000 questions, and OpenFactQA contains 1,000 questions as well. Every condition was applied to the same questions in each dataset.

The hallucination frequency is the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts. BLEU measures n-gram overlap with the reference answer. The latency is the mean number of seconds needed to produce an answer.
